cards.front: What does continue outer; do to the labelled outer loop?
cards.back: Skips the rest of that loop's body and starts its next iteration
cards.extra: The current pass of the inner loop is abandoned, and control goes to the labelled loop's update (a for) or its condition (while, do) — not to the statement after the loop. That is what separates it from break outer;, which leaves the labelled loop entirely.
cards.example:
outer:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j == 1) continue outer;
        System.out.println(i + "," + j);
    }
// prints 0,0  1,0  2,0

cards.front: Which statements may a labelled continue target?
cards.back: Only a loop — for, while or do; a labelled block is rejected
cards.extra: A continuation has to advance a loop, so javac checks the label's statement is a loop and otherwise fails with not a loop label: x. break x; on that same block compiles, because a break may leave any labelled statement.
cards.example:
x: {
    while (true) continue x;   // error: not a loop label: x
}

cards.front: Can a labelled break leave a statement that is not a loop?
cards.back: Yes — any labelled statement, including a plain block
cards.extra: The label names a statement, not a loop, so break x; inside a labelled block exits at the block's closing brace and execution continues after it. Only continue insists its target is a loop.
cards.example:
x: {
    System.out.println(1);
    if (done) break x;
    System.out.println(2);
}
System.out.println(3);   // 2 is skipped when break x runs

cards.front: Can two nested statements carry the same label name?
cards.back: No — javac: label a already in use
cards.extra: A label's scope is the whole statement it labels, so a statement inside it may not declare that name again. Sibling statements may reuse a name, since neither is nested in the other.
cards.example:
a: {
    a: while (true) break;   // error: label a already in use
}

cards.front: How far does a label's scope extend?
cards.back: Only over the single statement it labels
cards.extra: Outside that statement the name no longer exists, so a later continue a; fails with undefined label: a. A label is compile-time bookkeeping only: it declares no variable, allocates nothing and costs nothing at run time.
cards.example:
a: {
    while (true) break;
}
while (true) continue a;   // error: undefined label: a
